warmup.q: Kafka keeps three copies of a partition of payments, on three computers. A program that writes payments asks to hear back only once "all" copies have each one (the setting is called acks=all). Then two of the computers fall behind, and Kafka stops counting them as keeping up. The program sends a new payment, and every other setting is at its default. What happens?
options: The write fails, because "all" means all three copies
The write succeeds as soon as the one copy still keeping up has it, because "all" means all the copies keeping up right now
The write waits until both slow computers have caught up
Kafka quietly stops waiting for any copy and answers at once
warmup.why: acks=all means every copy on the current list of copies that are keeping up, which Kafka calls the in-sync replicas (ISR). When the two followers drop off it, the list is the leader alone, so one copy on one disk is enough, and the program hears that its payment is safe. The setting that changes this is min.insync.replicas. Its default is 1, which allows the one-copy case. Set it to 2, and the leader refuses such writes instead, which is what the first option expects to happen by default. The last section works through both.

sections.h: Three copies of every partition, and one leader among them
sections.html:
The coffee-shop payments app sends every card payment to Kafka as a record: one message, with a key (here the account number) and a value (the payment itself). Kafka keeps the records of the payments topic, a named log, split into partitions. Each partition is a separate log with its own number, such as payments-0, and each record in it gets the next number in line, its offset. The program that runs Kafka on a computer is a broker. Until now, every partition lived on one broker's disk, as a row of files.

Now that disk dies. Or the computer restarts for an update, which takes a few minutes. While it's down, nobody can write to payments-0 or read it. If the disk is gone for good, so are the payments in it.

The shop in the opening had the fix: keep copies. One copy is the leader. Every write goes to it, and it decides the order. The other copies are followers, and each one copies the leader's log in the same order. One leader, many followers, the first lesson of the Replication track, built this design for databases, and Kafka uses it once per partition. Each copy is a replica, and the number of copies is the topic's replication factor. Three is the usual choice for data you care about, so each partition lives on three brokers.

A Kafka partition is already a log, so copying it is simple. Producers, the programs that write records, send every record to the partition's leader. Only the leader gives out offsets, so offset 7 means the same payment on every broker. Each follower keeps asking the leader for the records after the last one it has, with a fetch request. That's the same kind of request a consumer, a program that reads records, sends. The follower appends what comes back at the same offsets. Consumers read from the leader too.

Each replica has its own log end offset (LEO), the offset its next record will get. A log that holds offsets 0 to 4 has an LEO of 5. The leader's LEO moves first, and the followers catch up a few milliseconds later as their fetches return. Every fetch carries the follower's LEO, so the leader always knows how far each follower has got.

When should the leader tell a producer that a payment is safe? If it answers as soon as its own copy has it, the producer may hear "safe" a moment before the leader's disk dies, and the payment is lost. If it waits for every follower, one slow follower holds up every write. Kafka takes a middle path, and the path moves as followers slow down.

The leader keeps a list of the replicas that are keeping up with it, the in-sync replicas, or ISR. The leader is always on it. In the shop, the ISR is the people in the room. From the ISR, the leader works out the high watermark (HW): the smallest LEO among them. Every record below the HW is on every in-sync replica, and those records are called committed. In the shop, it's the line in the books up to which everyone in the room has finished copying.

The high watermark does two jobs. Consumers read only below it, so they never see a record that could vanish if the leader died. And it decides when a careful producer hears back. A producer chooses how long the leader should wait before it answers, with its acks setting (short for acknowledgements, the leader's answers). acks=1 means "answer once your own copy has it". acks=all means "answer once every in-sync replica has it", which is the moment the HW passes the record. acks=all has been the default since Kafka 3.0.

With 3 partitions and replication factor 3 on three brokers, each broker leads one partition and follows the other two, so the work of leading is shared. When a leader's broker fails, a follower takes over, but only one that has every committed record. A replica that missed some would make them disappear without any error, because its shorter log would become the truth. Electing such a replica is an unclean leader election. Kafka forbids it by default (unclean.leader.election.enable=false): the partition stops taking writes instead of losing data.

Someone has to choose which follower takes over, and everyone has to agree on the choice. Next, we'll meet the part of Kafka that makes that call.

sections.h: Who picks the new leader: the controllers and KRaft
sections.html:
Say the broker that leads payments-2 dies. One of its followers must take over, and only one. What if each broker decided for itself? After a short network fault, two followers could each think the leader was gone, both declare themselves leader and both accept writes. Each would give offset 500 to a different payment. Two leaders at once is called split brain, and it's how one log ends up with two histories.

So one part of the cluster must decide, and every broker must agree on what it decided. The Consistency and consensus track built the tool for this in Consensus with Raft. Raft is a set of rules that lets a few computers agree on a list of changes by majority vote. Its next lesson, Coordination services: ZooKeeper, etcd and KRaft, showed clusters keeping their shared facts in such a list.

Kafka's version is KRaft, its own implementation of Raft. A few nodes in the cluster are controllers. They keep the cluster's metadata: the facts about the cluster itself, not about payments. That means which brokers are alive, which topics and partitions exist, which broker leads each partition and which replicas are in its ISR. When a leader's broker dies, the controller picks a new leader from the ISR and tells every broker.

The controllers keep the metadata as a log of their own, the internal topic __cluster_metadata, with one partition. Every change is a record in it: a topic created, a broker declared dead, a new leader for payments-2. One controller is active, the Raft leader. It appends the changes, and the others, called voters, copy them. A change counts once a majority has it, two of three. That's why controllers come in odd numbers. Three survive one failure, and five survive two. Four still survive only one, because a majority of four is three.

If the active controller dies, the others elect a new one within a couple of seconds (controller.quorum.election.timeout.ms is 1 second). Each election raises a counter called the leader epoch, Raft's term number. Every node ignores orders that carry an older epoch, so a replaced controller that wakes up late can't cause trouble.

You may be thinking, "Then why not run Raft for every partition, too?" The reason is cost. A majority vote needs 2f + 1 copies to survive f failures: three copies to survive one. Kafka's design doc points out that with the ISR, f + 1 copies are enough, so two copies survive one failure without losing committed records. That's safe for two reasons. Every change to an ISR is written to the metadata log, which the controllers agree on with Raft. And a new leader only ever comes from the ISR. So Kafka votes on the small metadata log and uses the ISR for the big logs of data.

Brokers read the metadata log from the active controller and apply it, much as a consumer reads a topic. Each broker also sends the controller a heartbeat, a short "I'm alive" message, every 2 seconds (broker.heartbeat.interval.ms). If a broker misses heartbeats for 9 seconds (broker.session.timeout.ms), the controller fences it. It stops treating that broker as alive, removes it from every ISR and gives the partitions it led to in-sync followers. A broker that shuts down cleanly tells the controller first, so its partitions move at once.

In the shop, the controllers are a small committee of managers. When the owner is away, they decide who keeps the main book, and they write every decision in their own minutes. The picture bends in one place: the committee votes on its decisions, but nobody votes on the sales. The sales are copied, never voted on.

A node can be a broker, a controller or both (process.roles=broker,controller, called combined mode). The lab cluster runs three combined nodes, to save memory. Big clusters usually put the controllers on their own small machines, so a busy broker can't slow down the votes, and losing brokers never costs the controllers their majority.

Before Kafka 4.0, this metadata lived in a separate program, ZooKeeper. Kafka 3.9 was the last release that could use it, and since 4.0, KRaft is the only mode.

The controllers decide who leads each partition and who is in sync. Next, we'll see how a follower drops out of the ISR, and what that does to acks=all.

sections.h: What "all" means in acks=all, and the floor that makes it safe
sections.html:
Back to the shop, on a normal day. One assistant is in the room, but she writes very slowly, because her pen keeps running dry. Should the owner wait for her before she calls a sale done? If she always waits for everyone, one slow copier holds up every sale. If she never waits, a sale she called done can vanish with her book.

Kafka's answer is to wait for the ISR, and to drop followers that fall too far behind. A follower leaves the ISR in one of two ways. If its broker stops sending heartbeats, the controller fences the broker after 9 seconds and removes it from every ISR. If the broker is alive but the follower can't keep up, the leader removes it once it hasn't caught up to the leader's end for replica.lag.time.max.ms, 30 seconds by default. Fetching isn't enough: the follower has to reach the end. When it catches up to the high watermark again, it rejoins.

While a slow follower is still in the ISR, it holds the high watermark back, and every acks=all producer waits with it. Once the leader removes it, the HW jumps forward and the waiting producers get their answers. The stepper below goes through it one frame at a time.

Now the warm-up's question. acks=all doesn't mean all replicas. It means all replicas currently in the ISR. If the ISR shrinks to the leader alone, one copy on one disk satisfies acks=all. The producer hears that the payment is safe, and losing that one broker loses the payment. That's the shop with both assistants at home.

min.insync.replicas closes the gap. It's the smallest ISR size at which the leader accepts an acks=all write, the shop's rule of "no sale counts until at least two of us have copied it". It's a setting on the topic. Here's a program creating the payments topic with it, through Kafka's admin client, the part of the Kafka library that manages topics. NewTopic takes the name, the number of partitions and the replication factor:

Java
NewTopic payments = new NewTopic("payments", 3, (short) 3)          // 3 partitions, 3 replicas
        .configs(Map.of("min.insync.replicas", "2"));               // acks=all needs 2 in sync
admin.createTopics(List.of(payments)).all().get();
Kotlin
val payments = NewTopic("payments", 3, 3.toShort())                 // 3 partitions, 3 replicas
    .configs(mapOf("min.insync.replicas" to "2"))                   // acks=all needs 2 in sync
admin.createTopics(listOf(payments)).all().get()

With replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, the topic can lose one replica and keep taking writes, and every payment the producer was told is safe sits on at least two brokers. If the ISR drops to one, the leader refuses acks=all writes with the error NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS. The default is 1, which promises nothing of the kind. The KafkaProducer documentation recommends replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 for topics written with transactions (Transactions and exactly-once covers those), and it's the right setting for payments too.

acks=all waits for whoever is in sync. Set the floor so that's never one.

Two details catch people out. min.insync.replicas applies only to acks=all, so a producer with acks=1, which waits for the leader alone, writes straight past the floor. And NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS is a retriable error, one the producer expects to clear up if it tries again. So your send doesn't fail at once. The producer logs a warning and keeps retrying until delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes by default) runs out. Only then does it fail the send, with a TimeoutException, an error that says no more than "I gave up waiting". When you see those timeouts, look for NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS in the warnings.

The shop picture breaks here. An assistant who left the room can come back only after copying every line up to the high watermark. And it's the managers, not the owner, who decide who is in the room after a broker dies.

Copies protect the payments from a dead disk or a dead broker, and that's where today's idea stops. A producer still learns only "safe" or "gave up". What happens between its send() and that answer is the producer's side of the story, and the next two lessons open it up.

try.title: Lose a broker, then raise the bar
steps: Run the demo once with all three nodes up (command below, from the labs folder). It sends one payment with acks=all and prints the partition and offset where it landed.

Stop node 3 with docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml stop kafka-3. Describe the topic again (the second command of the first Try it) and run the demo. Which ISRs changed, and which partitions got a new leader?

Every ISR still has two members. Stopping a second node would also break the controllers' majority, because each node here is a controller too. So raise the bar instead: docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name payments --add-config min.insync.replicas=3. Predict what happens, then run the demo. Then run it again with -Pargs=1 added, for acks=1.
Start node 3 with docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml start kafka-3, wait a few seconds, describe the topic and run the demo once more.
Stop the cluster: docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml down -v.

With three nodes up: acks=all: written to partition 2 at offset 0. The key acct-17 always lands in partition 2; Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering shows why. After stopping node 3, broker 3 is gone from every ISR, and the partitions it led have new leaders:

	Topic: payments	Partition: 1	Leader: 1	Replicas: 1,2,3	Isr: 1,2	...

WARN ... Got error produce response with correlation id 7 on topic-partition payments-2, retrying (... attempts left). Error: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS

acks=all: refused with TimeoutException

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 design: replication, ISR and min.insync.replicas

aside.title: Why is min.insync.replicas set on the topic, not on the producer?
aside.html: Because it protects the data, not one writer. Many programs may write to payments, and every one of them should get the same floor. If each producer chose its own, one careless program could quietly write payments onto a single disk. So the producer can only ask for acks=all, and the topic (or the broker's default) decides how many in-sync copies that has to mean.

opening:
Picture a small shop that keeps three copies of its sales book. The owner writes each sale in her book, and two assistants copy it into theirs. The house rule says a sale counts once everyone in the room has copied it. One afternoon both assistants go home ill. The rule is still met: everyone in the room has copied every sale, because the room is the owner alone.

It's easy to read a rule like that as "three copies, always". The word "everyone" sounds absolute, and on a normal day it is. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages and lets other programs read them, has the same rule and the same gap.

Partitions and segments on disk showed each partition of a log living as files on one computer's disk. That left a question open: what happens when that disk dies? In this lesson, we'll copy each partition to three computers, see who decides which copy leads, and find out what "all" means in acks=all. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a shop whose rule, "everyone in the room has copied it", was met by the owner alone. Kafka's acks=all works the same way: it waits for whoever is in sync, and min.insync.replicas decides how few that may be.

Next time you start the lab cluster, describe a topic and compare Replicas with Isr. Then run kafka-configs.sh --describe on the topic and look for min.insync.replicas. A value of 1 on a topic that carries money is worth a question.

Next, we'll move to the program that writes the payments. We'll find out how it picks a partition for each one, and what that choice does to their order.

compare.title: A payments producer that waits for every in-sync copy, in Java and Kotlin

compare.note: Both build the same producer, the object a program uses to send records to Kafka. Kotlin passes a mapOf(... to ...), which fits the producer's constructor that takes a map of settings. Java code often still uses Properties, an older map of text settings, and both work. The ProducerConfig constants are names for the settings, so a typo in a key becomes a compile error instead of a setting Kafka quietly ignores. Notice what's missing from both: min.insync.replicas. It's a setting on the topic (or the broker), not on the producer. The producer can only ask for acks=all; the topic decides how many replicas that has to mean.

worked.title: Find partitions where acks=all writes are being refused

steps.say: Payments must never sit on a single copy. Say you want a check, run every minute by a small monitoring program, that flags partitions whose ISR is below min.insync.replicas. That's exactly when acks=all producers start timing out. Start by describing the topic. (admin is an Admin client, the part of the Kafka library that asks the cluster about its topics.)
steps.code: // 1. leader, replicas and ISR for every partition TopicDescription desc = admin.describeTopics(List.of("payments")) .allTopicNames().get().get("payments");

alt.html: // 1. leader, replicas and ISR for every partition val desc = admin.describeTopics(listOf("payments")) .allTopicNames().get().getValue("payments")

steps.say: Read the min.insync.replicas in force. It may be set on the topic, on the broker or for the whole cluster, and describeConfigs returns whichever value applies.
steps.code: // 2. the min.insync.replicas that applies to this topic var res = new ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "payments"); int minIsr = Integer.parseInt(admin.describeConfigs(List.of(res)).all().get() .get(res).get("min.insync.replicas").value());

alt.html: // 2. the min.insync.replicas that applies to this topic val res = ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "payments") val minIsr = admin.describeConfigs(listOf(res)).all().get() .getValue(res).get("min.insync.replicas").value().toInt()

steps.say: Sort each partition into one of two cases. An ISR smaller than the list of replicas means the partition is under-replicated: still safe, with less room for another failure. An ISR below min.insync.replicas means acks=all writes to that partition are being refused right now.
steps.code: // 3. classify every partition for (TopicPartitionInfo p : desc.partitions()) { int isr = p.isr().size(), replicas = p.replicas().size(); if (isr < minIsr) { System.out.printf("partition %d: ISR %d < min %d, acks=all writes refused%n", p.partition(), isr, minIsr); } else if (isr < replicas) { System.out.printf("partition %d: under-replicated, %d of %d in sync%n", p.partition(), isr, replicas); } }

alt.html: // 3. classify every partition for (p in desc.partitions()) { val isr = p.isr().size val replicas = p.replicas().size when { isr < minIsr -> println("partition ${p.partition()}: ISR $isr < min $minIsr, acks=all writes refused") isr < replicas -> println("partition ${p.partition()}: under-replicated, $isr of $replicas in sync") } }

steps.say: On the lab cluster with node 3 stopped and min.insync.replicas=3, every partition would land in the first case. A real system would report these two counts as metrics, numbers a monitoring tool graphs and raises alarms on, instead of printing them. Brokers publish the same numbers themselves (the under-replicated and under-min-ISR partition counts). This check is the version any program can run from the outside.

lab.title: Model the ISR and the high watermark
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. 12 of 13 fail for now; the one that passes only checks the constructor you were given. Skim ReplicatedPartitionTest: each test is one rule from this lesson. No Docker needed.

ReplicatedPartition.java models one partition and its replicas in memory. Write advanceHighWatermark first: the smallest LEO among the ISR members, never lower than the current HW. Everything else calls it.
Write append: refuse Acks.ALL with NotEnoughReplicasException when the ISR is smaller than minInsyncReplicas. Otherwise move the leader's LEO, advance the HW and return the last offset written.
Write fetch: set the follower's LEO, and record the time it caught up if it reached the leader's LEO. Let it rejoin the ISR once its LEO is at least the HW, then advance the HW.
Write shrinkIsr: remove followers that are behind the leader and haven't caught up for more than replicaLagTimeMaxMs, then advance the HW.
Run the tests until all 13 pass. Then reread the test about the default min.insync.replicas of 1 and say out loud why it passes.
hints: isr.stream().mapToLong(logEndOffset::get).min().orElseThrow() is the smallest LEO in the ISR. Wrap it in Math.max(highWatermark, ...) so the HW never moves back.

In shrinkIsr, isr.removeIf(...) takes a lambda, a small function written inline. Keep the leader out of it, and keep followers whose LEO already equals the leader's: on a quiet partition there's nothing new for them to fetch.

NotEnoughReplicasException is the real class from kafka-clients, Kafka's Java library, in org.apache.kafka.common.errors. On a real client, the broker's NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS error turns into this exception. Its constructor takes a message.

drill.title: Work out the high watermark from memory
drill.prompt: Leader 1 has LEO 120. Follower 2 has LEO 118 and is in the ISR. Follower 3 has LEO 90 and left the ISR a minute ago. min.insync.replicas is 2. Without looking back, answer: (a) What is the HW? (b) Which offsets can a consumer read? (c) Is an acks=all write accepted? Then write the HW update as one statement in Java or Kotlin, and compare.

answer.html: // (a) HW = smallest LEO in the ISR {1, 2} = min(120, 118) = 118. Follower 3 is out, so its 90 doesn't count. // (b) offsets below 118, that is up to 117 (whatever retention has kept). // (c) yes: the ISR has 2 members, and min.insync.replicas is 2. highWatermark = Math.max(highWatermark, isr.stream().mapToLong(logEndOffset::get).min().orElseThrow());

alt.html: // (a) HW = smallest LEO in the ISR {1, 2} = min(120, 118) = 118. Follower 3 is out, so its 90 doesn't count. // (b) offsets below 118, that is up to 117 (whatever retention has kept). // (c) yes: the ISR has 2 members, and min.insync.replicas is 2. highWatermark = maxOf(highWatermark, isr.minOf { logEndOffset.getValue(it) })

recap: Kafka keeps each partition on several brokers, usually three. One replica, the leader, takes every write and gives out the offsets; the followers fetch from it and copy its log in the same order.

The ISR is the list of replicas keeping up with the leader, and the leader is always on it. A follower drops off when its broker is fenced (9 seconds without heartbeats) or when it hasn't caught up for replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 seconds).
The high watermark is the smallest log end offset in the ISR. Records below it are committed, and consumers only ever read committed records.

The KRaft controllers decide who leads each partition and who is in sync. They keep those facts in the __cluster_metadata log and agree on it by majority vote with Raft, so run 3 or 5 of them. ZooKeeper has been gone since Kafka 4.0.

acks=all waits for the current ISR, which can be the leader alone. min.insync.replicas (default 1) sets the floor: use replication factor 3 with 2 for payments. Below the floor, acks=all writes get NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS, retried until a TimeoutException.

The limit: copies protect the payments from a dead disk, but a producer still learns only "safe" or "gave up". What happens between send() and that answer is the producer's side, which the next two lessons open.

explain.prompt: Someone on your team says: "We use acks=all, so every payment Kafka confirms is on three brokers, right?" Explain what acks=all really guarantees, and what you'd change.
explain.answer: Not quite. acks=all makes the leader wait until every replica currently in the ISR has the record, and the ISR shrinks whenever a follower hasn't caught up for 30 seconds or its broker is fenced. If the ISR is down to the leader, one copy on one disk is enough for acks=all, and with the default min.insync.replicas of 1 the leader accepts that. I'd set min.insync.replicas=2 on the payments topics, with replication factor 3. Then every confirmed payment is on at least two brokers, and when only one in-sync replica is left, the leader refuses acks=all writes instead of pretending. I'd also add an alarm for partitions below their minimum ISR, because producers only see those refusals as timeouts.

deeper.html:
Kafka 4.0 shipped the first part of KIP-966. (A KIP, a Kafka Improvement Proposal, is one of the numbered documents in which Kafka's developers propose a change.) It adds eligible leader replicas (ELR), and since Kafka 4.1 it's on by default for new clusters. The lab cluster has it: kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 describe lists eligible.leader.replicas.version at level 1.

ELR closes a gap in the rules above. Suppose the ISR shrinks below min.insync.replicas, the leader stops accepting acks=all writes, and then the leader dies. If the controller may pick only from the ISR, there may be no one left to pick, and an unclean election would lose data. With ELR, the controller remembers replicas that left the ISR while it was below min.insync.replicas and that still hold every committed record, and it can safely elect one of them. ELR also stops the high watermark from moving while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas. So the setting really becomes the minimum number of copies of every committed record. Jack Vanlightly checked the design with TLA+, a language for describing a system precisely enough that a tool can check every possible run (see Sources).

You can see it on the lab cluster. With min.insync.replicas=3 on payments, pausing broker 2 for about half a minute (docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml pause kafka-2, then unpause) made kafka-topics.sh --describe show Isr: 1,3 and Elr: 2: broker 2 had left the ISR but stayed a safe candidate. The describe command itself can hang for up to 30 seconds while a broker is paused.

Two rules from the ELR documentation: once ELR is on, set min.insync.replicas for the whole cluster rather than per broker, and expect a change to it to clear the ELR state.
